title: Earth Circumference at Latitude: Parallels
description: Compute the length of any parallel with Earth Circumference at Latitude — the full circle of a latitude line, and how fast it spins. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, New York's parallel (40.758°N) is a 30,399 km circle — nearly 10,000 km shorter than the equator's — and the ground there still spins eastward at about 789 mph.
quick_answer: Earth Circumference at Latitude computes the full length of the circle traced by a line of latitude on the WGS84 ellipsoid. Enter the latitude and read the parallel's circumference in kilometres or miles — the number behind rotation speeds, parallel distances and why east-west degrees shrink toward the poles.
steps_intro: Every parallel is a circle. Most are smaller than you think:

body.t: Divide the parallel's length by the sidereal day (23.9345 h) and you have the ground's eastward speed: 1,040 mph at the equator, 522 mph at 60°. This page supplies the numerator honestly.
Circumference ÷ 360 is the degree's true length at that latitude — the same number the longitude-distance tools use, derived here from the whole circle.
East-west routes ride parallels that shrink poleward — one reason northern great-circle routes look 'shorter' on the map: their parallels really are shorter.
The parallel's radius is N·cos φ on WGS84, not simply R·cos φ — the table below shows the ellipsoid's small refinement over the school sphere.
At 51.5072°N the circumference is 24,994.6 km — barely five eighths of the equator's 40,075.0 km. London circles the Earth's axis in a loop smaller than many people guess for the whole planet.
At 80° the parallel is just 6,981.7 km, and at the pole itself it collapses to a point: the only 'circumference' on Earth that fits in a snow footprint.

popular_table.title: Circumference of parallels (WGS84)
popular_table.intro: Computed as 2π × N(φ) × cos φ — the ellipsoid's own circles.
popular_table.note: Rotation speeds use the sidereal day (23 h 56 m) — the Earth's true spin period against the stars, which is what a parallel actually completes.

faq: Why is it not just 40,075 × cos(latitude)?

That is the sphere's answer — close, but the ellipsoid's parallel radius uses the prime-vertical radius N(φ), which is slightly larger than R·cos φ implies. The difference peaks at mid-latitudes at a few hundred metres over the whole circle.
Is the equator's circumference the largest?
Yes — 40,075.017 km on WGS84, the greatest parallel. (The meridian ellipse is slightly smaller, 40,007.9 km around — the flattening again.)
The parallel becomes a point and the circumference zero — the formula's honest limit, and the reason 'east' stops meaning anything at the pole itself.
Perfectly symmetric on the ellipsoid model: −45° prices exactly like +45°. Practical differences between hemispheres are geography, not geometry.
Can I get the parallel's radius instead?
Divide by 2π: at the equator that is 6,378.1 km (the semi-major axis); at 45°, about 4,517 km from the axis — the distance that sets the rotation speed.
Why sidereal day for rotation speed?

The ground returns to the same orientation against the stars in 23 h 56 m 4 s; the extra four minutes to face the Sun again is orbital motion, not spin. Circumference over sidereal day is the physical speed.
Trivially — a parallel flown at 11 km is about 69 km longer around (2π × 11 km), which is why the number that matters for aircraft is the ground track's, stated here.
